extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, communications professionals, and journalism/PR students
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the ethical codes and standards used to guide professional conduct in public relations (PRSA, IABC, IPRA), including core values, provisions/commitments, enforcement notes, and their application to modern dilemmas such as AI and digital misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: PRSA: Six Core Values
rubrics_metrics.description: The PRSA Code is grounded in six core values that represent the fundamental beliefs of the profession: Advocacy; Honesty; Expertise; Independence; Loyalty; Fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each value carries specific meaning: Advocacy — serve the public interest as responsible advocates (not propaganda); Honesty — uphold highest standards of accuracy and truth; Expertise — continually develop skills via research and education; Independence — provide objective counsel and avoid compromises to professional judgment; Loyalty — be faithful to clients but balance against public interest; Fairness — deal fairly with all stakeholders and respect diverse opinions. These values are the foundational evaluative standards for PR behaviour and messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: PRSA: Provisions of Conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: PRSA includes six provisions of conduct paired with core principles, stated intent, and examples of improper behaviour covering areas such as the free flow of information, competition, disclosure of information, safeguarding confidences, and avoiding conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: giving expensive gifts to a journalist to influence coverage violates disclosure provisions; representing competing clients without disclosing the conflict breaches safeguarding confidences. The provisions are practical, with real-world examples to guide day-to-day practice. The PRSA Board of Ethics and Professional Standards issues Professional Standards Advisories (PSAs) on emerging issues (social media, native advertising, AI). Note: the PRSA Code is aspirational; enforcement is internal (membership revocation or expulsion) rather than legal.

rubrics_metrics.name: IABC: Three Foundational Principles and Core Standards
rubrics_metrics.description: IABC frames its code around three interrelated principles that assume respect for human rights and the rule of law, organisational agreement on right/wrong criteria, and sensitivity to cultural norms. From these, IABC derives three core standards: professional communication must be legal, it must be ethical, and it must be in good taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This orientation highlights legal compliance and cultural sensitivity as integral to ethical communication. 'In good taste' signals attention to cultural norms and matters of taste when judging content and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: IABC: 11 Articles / Member Commitments
rubrics_metrics.description: The IABC Code outlines 11 specific commitments members must embrace, including acting honestly, communicating accurate information, promptly correcting errors, protecting confidential information, supporting free speech, respecting cultural values, giving proper credit, and avoiding use of confidential information for personal gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable practical provisions: members must not represent conflicting or competing interests without full written disclosure and consent; communicators must not guarantee results beyond their power to deliver (guards against overpromising). All IABC members sign a statement affirming they have reviewed and understand the code. An Ethics Committee of accredited professionals provides advice and professional development support.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPRA: Rights-based grounding of the Code
rubrics_metrics.description: IPRA's Code of Conduct is explicitly rooted in international human rights instruments (UN Charter, the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights, especially Article 19 on freedom of opinion and expression), giving the code a global and rights-based character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Code consolidates historic documents (Code of Venice, Athens, Brussels) and emphasizes the moral obligation of PR practitioners to respect fundamental human dignity when influencing public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPRA: 18 Principles (integrity, accuracy, confidentiality, financial ethics, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The consolidated IPRA Code outlines 18 specific principles covering integrity and transparency; accuracy and truthfulness; confidentiality; fair dealing; and financial ethics, among others. It also includes provisions relevant to the digital age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/expectations: act honestly and openly declare identity and interests represented; take reasonable steps to ensure information is correct and promptly correct errors; honour confidential information shared by clients; avoid deceptive practices (front organisations, dishonest client poaching, intentionally damaging competitors); avoid undisclosed payments or offering inducements to public officials or media; do not sell for profit documents obtained from public authorities. The code recognises rapid spread of misinformation online and was reviewed (2020) as still fit for modern challenges. Violations can lead to membership consequences but the code is largely aspirational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common themes across PRSA, IABC, and IPRA
rubrics_metrics.description: All three codes share recurring themes and evaluative criteria: honesty, accuracy, confidentiality, fairness, and accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences in emphasis: PRSA is detailed and practical (U.S.-centric) with provisions and PSAs; IABC is broader, aimed at business communicators worldwide with clear personal-commitment language; IPRA is the most globally aspirational and rights-oriented. When evaluating PR outputs (press releases, campaigns), these common themes form the baseline checklist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforceability, Scope, and Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional PR codes are primarily aspirational and voluntary; they are self-regulatory rather than legally enforceable. Organisations reserve rights to bar or expel members but there are typically no legal penalties tied to code violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations: enforcement depends on peer accountability and willingness to act; codes only bind members of the respective organisations (many practitioners are non-members); rapid technological change (digital communication, AI, data privacy) can outpace guideline updates. These constraints should be considered when relying on codes for compliance or public assurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics Education and Professional Development
rubrics_metrics.description: Codes are supported by ethics education initiatives: PRSA designates Ethics Month and requires accredited members (APR) to complete continuing education units focused on ethics; IABC supports ethics-related professional development through its Ethics Committee; IPRA offers Thought Leadership essays and webinars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ongoing education is presented as a mechanism to keep practitioners aligned with evolving ethical expectations and to strengthen the profession's credibility; adherence to codes can be signalled to clients as a competitive advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to specific ethical dilemmas in press releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Codes provide practical guidance for concrete dilemmas—for example, omitting negative product safety data from a press release would violate PRSA's emphasis on honest communication and public interest; IABC's accuracy/legal requirements and IPRA's accuracy principle similarly prohibit such omissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use codes as decision tools: when a client requests omission or deception, codes advise practitioners to push back. These principles apply directly to press-release content choices, disclosures, and claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about AI and digital-era responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Codes address digital-era challenges such as AI-generated content, social media ethics, native advertising, and the rapid viral spread of misinformation—calling for transparency, accuracy, and responsible use of new tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRSA issues Professional Standards Advisories on emerging issues like AI; IPRA has an AI Chapter to provide guidance. Practical expectations include being transparent about machine-generated content (who created the content), verifying accuracy, and clearly disclosing any sponsored/native formats to avoid misleading audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of Interest, Disclosure, and Safeguarding Confidences
rubrics_metrics.description: All codes emphasise avoiding conflicts of interest: disclose competing client relationships and obtain consent; safeguard client confidences; disclose meaningful financial relationships and gifts to media or officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical anti-patterns: accepting undisclosed payments, giving gifts to influence coverage, representing competing clients without disclosure. Codes require written disclosure/consent for conflicting representations and expect transparent handling of confidential information.
